description: Reference points for m4 SA on organometallics, and the correction of a severity claim made earlier today.
why: I called SA=7.37 'the worst metric, ~2x outside the usable range' by comparing it to the organic drug-like scale (2-3). That comparison is not valid for organometallics.
FINDING: A clinically used drug (cisplatin, PubChem canonical charged form) scores SA 7.467 — the same band as our generated organometallics. Organic drug-like molecules score 1.0-3.1. So SA=7 is not evidence of broken chemistry; it is evidence that the Ertl scale was calibrated on organic libraries and organometallics sit outside its domain, where the fragment-rarity term bites hardest.

visible_drivers_within_our_own_data.size: corr(SA, heavy atom count) = +0.274 (blk_c5_repair) / +0.480 (fm_ab) / +0.459 (frag_control). The best-SA run generates the SMALLEST molecules (35.4 vs 39.3 heavy atoms).
visible_drivers_within_our_own_data.fragmentation: NOT the driver. blk_c5_repair has both the fewest fragments (3.52) and the lowest SA; fm_ab has the most fragments (10.04) but a mid SA. My earlier 'lower SA means more fragmented' was an artifact of comparing a different-batch n=147 run against the others.

honest_remaining_uncertainty: Our molecules are ~39 heavy atoms, 4-5x cisplatin's 8, so size alone accounts for part of the gap — but a 39-atom organic molecule would score ~2-3, not 7.9. So there is likely a real component beyond pure domain mismatch. NOT quantified: what fraction of the 6.66-7.93 band is size, fragment rarity, or genuinely poor chemistry.
not_a_metric_fix_yet: Recorded as a scale-comparability finding. No code changed. Deciding whether to define an organometallic-specific SA reference would need tmQM molecules scored through RDKit, which failed to construct (metal valences) — that is itself worth a follow-up.
